card.hook: Here's a photo shoot where the models walk right up to you. Keepers lead baby elephants to a rope line, and some of them arrive covered in reddish mud.
card.stand_here: Start at the phone icon on the map, about 170 m south-west of the Trust's elephant orphanage in Nairobi National Park, and face north-east. It's about 3 minutes on foot. Once you're inside the viewing area, walk in and stand on the left-hand side.
card.zoom: Use 1x for the big scene: keepers, calves and the rope line all together. Switch to 2x when an orphan walks up for a close-up portrait. They come so close that you won't need a big zoom, and 0.5x is only worth a try if the group gets really near.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the elephant on one third of the frame, with a keeper or the rope line filling the rest.
card.best_time: The public can only visit for one hour a day, so get there early to claim a good spot at the rope. Our notes say that hour runs 11:00 to 12:00 and booking is a must, so check the official site before you go.
card.selfie_here: Try the left-hand side of the viewing area as you walk in, where a Nairobi tour blog says the elephants usually make their entrance. Use the front camera, hold it a little low, and let the calves and keepers fill the background behind your shoulder. Or use the rope barrier along one edge of the play area, where keepers bring the calves after football and mud baths.
card.rules_and_safety: Stay behind the rope and keep your flash off. During the mud bath a calf can spray bystanders with a trunkful of mud, so stay alert.
card.challenge: Catch a calf mid-roll in the mud, then see if you can get a keeper in the same shot, looking suitably unbothered.
card.good_to_know: Dame Daphne Sheldrick founded the Trust in 1977 to honour her late husband, David, a naturalist and the founding warden of Tsavo East National Park. It was called the David Sheldrick Wildlife Trust until February 2019, when the name changed to honour both of them. Orphaned calves are rescued from across Kenya, raised here, and later returned to the wild.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Start at the phone icon on the map, about 170 m south-west of the Trust's elephant orphanage in Nairobi National Park, and face north-east. It's about 3 minutes on foot. Once you're inside the viewing area, walk in and stand on the left-hand side.

card.hook: Picture a zebra grazing on open grass while city buildings sit on the horizon behind it. That's Nairobi National Park, and yes, it really is that close to town.
card.stand_here: Stand on Impala Viewpoint, the hilltop near the Main Gate, on the highest point. Face across the plains towards the open park area, with the Nairobi skyline in the distance.
card.zoom: Animals are usually far away, so try zoom 2x to 5x, depending on your phone. Go back to 1x for plains with trees, and use 0.5x when you want big sky and wide views.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the animal on the screen, then slide the picture a little darker if the sky is bright.
card.best_time: The dry season is when you're most likely to see animals, because they gather around the small dams along the river. On any day, early morning and late afternoon usually give softer light and calmer animals.
card.selfie_here: Try Impala Observation Point: climb the raised platform, a short walk up from a vehicle stop on the plains circuit, and turn so the open plains are behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x to fit more landscape in, or try the Ivory Burning Site Monument, about 10 minutes from the main gate, with the grassland stretching out behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Follow park staff instructions and never leave your vehicle to get closer to an animal. On the Hippo Pools walk a ranger escort is mandatory, and you must stay on the marked path. One guide says Impala Observation Point is closed on weekends, so check before you go.
card.challenge: Get an acacia, a few grazing animals and a slice of open grass in one frame, so your photo says 'I was really there'.
card.good_to_know: Nairobi National Park opened in 1946 and was Kenya's first national park. It covers about 117 square kilometres, roughly 7 km from the centre of Nairobi. It's known as one of Kenya's most successful rhino sanctuaries, and up to 500 bird species have been recorded here too.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Impala Viewpoint, the hilltop near the Main Gate, on the highest point. Face across the plains towards the open park area, with the Nairobi skyline in the distance.

card.hook: Giraffes here are so tall and so close that your phone has to look up, and a warthog might trot through the background while you do. Go low, shoot up, and let the necks reach into the greenery.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, in the lower feeding area of the garden, about 180 m west of the subject, and face east. Step back until a whole giraffe fits in the frame.
card.zoom: Use zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for full-body giraffe portraits without crowding the animals. Switch to 1x when you want the garden around them, and save 0.5x for a very close head-and-neck shot.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the giraffe's body on one line and leave some room above its head so the neck doesn't look chopped off.
card.best_time: Go in the morning, when the light is soft. Midday sun is harsh and makes everything look flat.
card.selfie_here: Climb the raised wooden feeding platform, where a giraffe's head is at eye level right behind you. Use the front camera, and one guide suggests standing on the far left, where the giraffes come over first.
card.ask_someone: Stand in the lower garden below the feeding platform and ask a passer-by to shoot you from a little way off, so the giraffes tower above you.
card.rules_and_safety: Skip the flash, as it can startle the animals, and drones aren't allowed anywhere on the property. Don't climb down from the platform toward the giraffes, because frustrated giraffes may headbutt. Keep your phone strap round your wrist near the animals.
card.challenge: Get one full-height giraffe shot with a warthog photobombing in the background.
card.good_to_know: The Giraffe Centre in Lang'ata protects the Rothschild's giraffe, a species found only in the grasslands of East Africa. Jock Leslie Melville and his wife Betty started a breeding programme here in 1979, and it opened to visitors by 1983. It's a paid site and the viewing areas may have changed, so check the official site before you go.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, in the lower feeding area of the garden, about 180 m west of the subject, and face east. Step back until a whole giraffe fits in the frame.

selfie_spots.why: The platform brings you to giraffe head height, so the animals fill the frame right behind your face.

card.hook: Picture a huge round concrete drum with flower beds and flagpoles lined up at its feet. That's the KICC, and it's one of the easiest towers in Africa to fit on a small screen.
card.stand_here: Head for City Square, on the plaza in front of the main tower entrance, just off Harambee Avenue. The map spot is about 400 m away, so face the tower from there and let it stand tall as a landmark. At the plaza itself, the drum can fill the frame.
card.zoom: From the map spot about 400 m away, use zoom 1x or 2x so the tower sits nicely in the scene. Down at the close plaza, switch to zoom 0.5x only if the drum won't fit. Save zoom 5x for a tight shot of the concrete texture or the top of the tower.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest part of the concrete, then slide it a little darker so the texture shows and the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Go in the afternoon, when the sun lights up the textured concrete. For the Uhuru Park view, a clear morning gives you the best chance of spotting the Ngong Hills far off to the south-west.
card.selfie_here: Take it on the fountain walkway to the main entrance (City Hall side), on the path between the fountains as you head toward the tower. Use the front camera, hold it a bit low, and let the tower rise behind you. If your front camera has a 0.5x button, try it to fit more in.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the paved courtyard by the seated Jomo Kenyatta statue, with the tower in view behind them, while you pose beside the statue.
card.rules_and_safety: Phone photos on the rooftop are allowed at no extra cost. Bring a passport or photo ID to enter the building, because security is tight. The rooftop deck is paid, run separately, and can close at short notice, so check before you plan around it.
card.challenge: Turn on gridlines, line the drum's edges up with the vertical lines, then snap one upright shot with flagpoles along the bottom. Bonus points if the flags look like they're guarding the tower.
card.good_to_know: The KICC is a 32-storey landmark, and its main tower is a round drum of just over 105 metres. President Jomo Kenyatta commissioned it in 1967, and it was finished in 1973. For years it was the tallest building in Kenya, and its light terracotta finish is meant to echo traditional African architecture.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for City Square, on the plaza in front of the main tower entrance, just off Harambee Avenue. The map spot is about 400 m away, so face the tower from there and let it stand tall as a landmark. At the plaza itself, the drum can fill the frame.

card.hook: Most people snap the front of the farmhouse and wander off, but the back lawn is where it gets good. Green grass rolls out in front of you, and the Ngong Hills rise behind it like a painted backdrop.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, then follow the paths round to the back lawn of the house. Face the Ngong Hills for the big view, or turn around to catch the house from the rear.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the house and lawn. Go to 0.5x when you want the whole house, lawn and sky in one shot, and try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pull the hills closer.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines so the roofline and the line of the hills sit level, then tap the hills and slide darker if the sky looks washed out.
card.best_time: Go in the morning, when the sun is behind you as you look toward the hills, according to one guide.
card.selfie_here: Try the veranda, facing the garden with the Ngong Hills beyond, or the front lawn with the farmhouse behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x and hold it a bit lower so the house fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand back on the front lawn, far enough that the whole farmhouse and its veranda fit in the frame, with you standing in front of the house.
card.rules_and_safety: Skip photos inside the house: most sources say no photography indoors, and flash isn't allowed, so ask a staff member when you arrive. The grounds are grassy and uneven, so wear walking shoes.
card.challenge: Find a spot where the red-tiled roofline peeks out between two tree trunks, then bag a bonus point if a jacaranda is blooming in the foreground.
card.good_to_know: The museum is a farmhouse with a wide lawn, mature trees and a view across to the Ngong Hills. The veranda makes a natural frame for the lawn and hills, and jacaranda blossom adds a splash of colour when it's out. Entry arrangements and fees for the grounds and house may differ, so check the official site before you go.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, then follow the paths round to the back lawn of the house. Face the Ngong Hills for the big view, or turn around to catch the house from the rear.

card.hook: Round mud walls, steep thatched roofs and a whole lot of green: Bomas of Kenya is one of those places where almost every corner looks good on your phone. Even the huge auditorium joins in.
card.stand_here: Stand at Millennium Hall and face west, looking back across the distance toward the site. Once you've got the view, step a little left or right to find the clearest line of sight and keep fences and parked vehicles out of the frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to catch the whole scene. Then try 2x or 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) to pick out a single hut or the texture of the thatch. Use 0.5x only if you're close to a big building and need to squeeze it all in.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the roofline on the upper third, and tap the roofs so they look right, then slide a touch darker if the sky is washing out.
card.best_time: Go in the morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and the shadows on the thatch and walls are gentler.
card.selfie_here: Try the Luo village homestead area with the traditional huts behind you. Hold your phone at arm's length with the front camera, and use 0.5x if your phone has it to fit more of the huts in. Nobody has confirmed this as a selfie spot, so check the layout when you arrive.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally allowed in the homestead section and during the show, but skip the flash during performances. Ask performers before taking close-ups of them. Bomas was temporarily closed for renovation in March 2025, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find the best roof in the village and fill the whole frame with its thatch, with no people walking through.
card.good_to_know: 'Bomas' means homesteads, and the site shows traditional homes of several Kenyan communities. It opened in October 1971 and sits about 10 km from the city centre, near Nairobi National Park. The Bomas Harambee Dancers have performed here since 1973. Because of the renovation and the planned new convention centre, it may look different from older pictures.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at Millennium Hall and face west, looking back across the distance toward the site. Once you've got the view, step a little left or right to find the clearest line of sight and keep fences and parked vehicles out of the frame.

card.hook: Picture a wide open courtyard, leafy grounds all around, and a whole museum front lined up across the space like it's waiting for its photo. That's the Great Court at Nairobi National Museum, and it's an easy win.
card.stand_here: Head for the Great Court, the open courtyard in front of the museum building, and face the front facade across the open space. Step back until the whole front fits on your screen.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the facade. Only switch to 0.5x if you truly can't step back any further, and keep the building in the middle so the edges don't stretch.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the walls up with them so the building stands nice and straight.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning or late in the afternoon, when the low sun gives the walls longer shadows and more shape. Keep the sun behind or beside you, not in front of you.
card.selfie_here: Do it in the Great Court, on the open paved courtyard facing the main facade. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to squeeze more building in, and keep the museum over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand back across the Great Court so the full facade fits, while you stand in the courtyard with the building behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally allowed in most galleries without flash, but ask staff if you're unsure. Professional photography or filming may need special permission and a permit from the museum.
card.challenge: Get the walls dead straight on the gridlines, with a long morning or evening shadow in the shot. Bonus points if you stay out of everyone else's photo.
card.good_to_know: The museum began in 1910 as a natural history society's collection. It opened as the Coryndon Museum in 1930 and took its present name in 1964, after independence. It reopened in June 2008 after a major rebuild.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the Great Court, the open courtyard in front of the museum building, and face the front facade across the open space. Step back until the whole front fits on your screen.

card.hook: Picture a calm lake, a few trees at the edge, and Nairobi's towers standing up behind them like they're photobombing your holiday snap. That's Uhuru Park, right next to the city centre.
card.stand_here: Stand in Uhuru Park at the water's edge on the lakeside and face across the lake so the skyline rises behind the trees. Follow the paths towards the lake once you're inside the park.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the lake with the skyline behind. Try 0.5x for more water and sky, or 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to bring the towers closer so they look bigger behind the trees.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the skyline, then slide the brightness down a little if the sky is washing out.
card.best_time: Go early, ideally before 9:00 AM, when the light is softer and it's quieter. Plan to leave before dusk.
card.selfie_here: Head to the southern hill at the south end of the park, on the rise facing back across the city. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and turn so the KICC tower stands tall over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: The park is very open, so take care moving around, and one visitor says street kids can make it feel insecure. The area is reported to be less safe after dark. Entry is reported as free with a national ID, so check the official site for current entry and photography rules before you go (professional shoots need a permit).
card.challenge: Find a warthog or rhino sculpture on the lawn and make it the star of your foreground, with the city behind it.
card.good_to_know: Uhuru Park covers 12.9 hectares (32 acres) and opened to the public on 23 May 1969. It closed in November 2021 and reopened on 30 March 2024 after renovation, so some features may have changed since older photos were taken.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Uhuru Park at the water's edge on the lakeside and face across the lake so the skyline rises behind the trees. Follow the paths towards the lake once you're inside the park.

selfie_spots.name: Southern hill at the south end of Uhuru Park
selfie_spots.detail: on the rise at the park's southern end, facing back across the CBD toward downtown
selfie_spots.why: The hill gives a clear sightline back over the central business district, with the KICC tower standing tall in the frame.

selfie_research.safety: A Tripadvisor reviewer says the park is very open, so visitors should be careful moving around, and notes street kids can make it feel insecure.

The hill spot is named as a southern hill, not a marked point, so it may need a local check. The SillySuitcase 'Uhuru Park View Point' (Cathedral Rd) is a viewpoint over the park rather than a spot with the park behind the visitor, so I left it out. A Google Local Guides post says photography in Nairobi is allowed only on Sundays; it is old, unverified, and not about selfie sticks or tripods, so I did not list it as a rule. No page I found states selfie stick or tripod rules.

card.hook: Picture a crisp white mosque with twin minarets and three silver domes, sitting in the middle of Nairobi's busy city centre. It's one of those buildings that looks good on your phone with almost no effort.
card.stand_here: Stand on Banda Street, on the pavement beside the mosque's south side, the street front. Face the mosque so both minarets and all three domes fit in one frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the straight-on front. If the minarets get cut off, tap 0.5x. For the domes and the tops of the minarets, try 2x or 5x, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the white front, then slide it a little darker so the walls keep their detail and the silver domes don't glare.
card.best_time: Go on a weekday, early or late in the day, for a clearer view of the front. Friday prayers bring crowds, so skip Fridays if you can.
card.selfie_here: Use the Banda Street pavement beside the mosque's south side. Switch to the front camera, use 0.5x if your phone has it, and tuck the white front with its minarets and domes behind your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Banda Street pavement opposite the mosque's south side, so the whole building fits, while you stand on the pavement beside the mosque. The exact spot is approximate, so adjust it on the ground.
card.rules_and_safety: It's a working place of worship, so avoid photographing during prayer times, especially Friday prayers. Ask before photographing anyone at prayer, ask permission before taking photos inside, and don't use flash.
card.challenge: Turn on the gridlines and line up both minarets with the vertical lines so neither one leans, with a little sky above the domes.
card.good_to_know: Glasgow architect William Landels designed Jamia Mosque, and it was built between 1925 and 1933. The style borrows from seventeenth-century Mughal mosques like the Jama Masjid in Delhi and the Badshahi Mosque in Lahore. It opened on 18 August 1933, when it was the tallest building in Nairobi, paid for by a long community fundraising drive.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Banda Street, on the pavement beside the mosque's south side, the street front. Face the mosque so both minarets and all three domes fit in one frame.

The ask-someone spot uses the same street as the selfie spot, since no page names a separate place. The Wikimedia photo location (-1.284083, 36.820694) is very close to the given position. card.hook: Picture a clock tower rising over a calm lake with Nairobi's skyline stacked up behind it. It's meant to remind you of Big Ben, and from across the water it does the job.
card.stand_here: Stand in Uhuru Park, on the lakeside, and face the Parliament clock tower across the water. Keep to the park and the public road, and don't walk up to the buildings.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the lake, tower and skyline in one frame. Then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the clock tower. Zoom 0.5x makes the tower look small, so save it for when you want lots of lake and sky.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line so it doesn't lean, then tap the tower and slide the brightness down a little if the sky looks washed out.
card.best_time: Morning or later afternoon usually gives softer light than the middle of the day. Take a few frames in a row, because people and joggers wander through the park.
card.selfie_here: The only selfie spot we found is on the public pavement side of the railings along the Parliament frontage in City Square, and it's low confidence because cameras are meant to stay down there. Ask local security first, and if they say yes, use the front camera with the clock tower over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography at Parliament is described as forbidden unless you have written permission, and security around it is real, so check with local security before you raise your phone. Along Harambee Avenue, keep your camera down.
card.challenge: If photos are okay on the day, get the lake in the lower third and the tower just off-centre, with the skyline peeking out behind it.
card.good_to_know: The Parliament Buildings went up in 1954 for the colonial Legislative Council and were called the Legislative Buildings until 1963. The English-style clock tower was a design requirement, so the buildings would echo the Palace of Westminster and Big Ben. Kenya's first president, Jomo Kenyatta, is buried on the estate.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Uhuru Park, on the lakeside, and face the Parliament clock tower across the water. Keep to the park and the public road, and don't walk up to the buildings.

selfie_spots.detail: on the public pavement side of the railings, looking at the clock tower and Parliament frontage across the City Square paving
selfie_spots.why: It is the only viewpoint a guide names for the clock tower and frontage, but the same guide warns that cameras should stay down along Harambee Avenue, so treat it as a low-confidence option.

card.hook: Most parks are laid out to look pretty. This one was laid out for trees, and that's exactly why your phone loves it: trunks and branches close in on both sides and frame the shot for you.
card.stand_here: Stand on Arboretum Drive at the main gate, by the entrance near Kenya Girl Guides Headquarters. Face into the grounds so the line of trees leads your eye inwards.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the gate view. Switch to 0.5x for the fig tree's canopy and the tall bamboo. Try 2x to 5x when you want to pick out a detail in the branches without leaving the path.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the entrance path or the line of trunks on the centre line, then tap the brightest trunk and slide darker a touch so the sunny patches don't wash out.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning or late in the afternoon. The light under the trees is at its softest then.
card.selfie_here: Stand beneath the big fig tree close to the middle of the grounds, with the canopy behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and hold your phone a little low so the branches fill the top of the frame. The open grass just inside the main gate also works, with the trees behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Phone photos are free, but paid or commercial shoots need a permit, so check the official site before you go. Paths can be muddy in places, and there are monkeys, so keep your phone and snacks secure and don't feed them.
card.challenge: Find the fig tree, step back until its canopy fills the whole screen, then see if you can spot a monkey keeping an eye on your snacks.
card.good_to_know: Nairobi Arboretum is in Kilimani. It was founded in 1907 by Mr. Batiscombe, who wanted to try out new forestry trees. It was gazetted as a national reserve in 1932.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Arboretum Drive at the main gate, by the entrance near Kenya Girl Guides Headquarters. It's a short walk or ride from the phone icon. Face into the grounds so the line of trees leads your eye inwards.

card.hook: Picture a 1913 stone building holding its ground while glass office towers crowd in behind it. That clash of old and new is the whole picture here, and it's a good one.
card.stand_here: Stand on the pavement at the corner of Kenyatta Avenue and Uhuru Highway and face east, because the gallery is to the east of you. Check the map for your exact pavement spot.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole front and some skyline. The building is about 49 metres across, so step back a little too. Switch to 1x for a more natural, less stretched look, then try 2x for details like the doorway and windows.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines and keep the building's vertical edges parallel to them so the walls don't lean, with the gallery on one side and the towers filling the other.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the stonework than the middle of the day. It's a busy city corner, so take a few frames and pick the cleanest one.
card.selfie_here: Head to the Point Zero marker just outside the building, by the original entrance, and stand on it with the gallery facade behind you. Use your front camera, and if it has a 0.5x button, try it to squeeze more of the building in over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Photographing the outside from the public pavement is fine. If you go inside, skip the flash and follow the museum's guidelines, and check the official site or ask at the desk before you go.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot and one close-up of the doorway, then see if you can spot the exact moment when no cars or people wander through the frame.
card.good_to_know: The building was designed by C. Rand Ovary and finished in 1913 as a government office. It became a national monument in 1995 and passed to the National Museums of Kenya in 1997. It opened as a gallery in 2005 and now shows African art.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the pavement at the corner of Kenyatta Avenue and Uhuru Highway and face east, because the gallery is to the east of you. Check the map for your exact pavement spot.

selfie_spots.why: Many visitors photograph themselves at this marker, which is the one feature the sources repeatedly single out as a photo draw at the gallery.

card.hook: Traffic rushes along Kenyatta Avenue, but across the road All Saints' Cathedral just sits there, solid and calm, with Uhuru Park's greenery nearby. It's a tidy, honest street shot, and it's easy to get right.
card.stand_here: Face north-east, toward the cathedral's street-facing front.
card.zoom: From the phone icon, zoom 5x (2x to 5x, depending on your phone) so the cathedral doesn't shrink to a tiny shape. Once you're on the pavement directly opposite the front, drop to 1x for the full view, then use zoom 2x for close-ups of the stonework and entrance.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the front up with the vertical lines so the building stands straight instead of leaning.
card.best_time: A weekday is calmer than Sunday, when services bring crowds and security queues. Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera and switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, so the cathedral fits over your shoulder. Hold the phone a little low and tilt it up to catch more of the building.
card.rules_and_safety: Stick to exterior photos from the public pavement. It's a place of worship, and photography inside is restricted and needs permission.
card.challenge: Get the cathedral front perfectly straight on the gridlines with a clear foreground. Wait for the gap between cars and passers-by, then take three frames and pick the winner.
card.good_to_know: A public meeting in 1914 raised money for a permanent church in the city centre. Temple Moore was the architect, and the foundation stone was laid on 3 February 1917. It became the Cathedral of the Highlands in 1924 and was consecrated in 1952. In the early 1990s, mothers of political prisoners held a long vigil here, and the prisoners were released in early 1993.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the public pavement of Kenyatta Avenue, opposite the Nairobi Serena Hotel; the cathedral is about 529 m from the phone icon. Face north-east, toward the cathedral's street-facing front.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a spot for a selfie with All Saints' Cathedral behind the visitor, or a spot for a passer-by to photograph the visitor with the whole cathedral. Pages mention that the cathedral stands on Kenyatta Avenue beside Uhuru Park (https://www.tripadvisor.com/Attraction_Review-g294207-d8131443-Reviews-All_Saints_Cathedral-Nairobi.html), and that Uhuru Park is next door (https://www.gpsmycity.com/attractions/all-saints-cathedral-22027.html), but none of them says where to stand for a photo. I did not add a spot from memory. Photography inside the cathedral is restricted and needs special permission, per https://www.tripadvisor.com/Attraction_Review-g294207-d8131443-Reviews-or20-All_Saints_Cathedral-Nairobi.html and https://mindtrip.ai/attraction/nairobi-kenya/all-saints-cathedral-nairobi/at-Lw6qBgJS. Those pages describe the indoor rule, not selfie sticks or tripods, so I have not listed it under rules. Suggest checking the grounds on arrival or searching for a Uhuru Park or Kenyatta Avenue photo guide.

card.hook: Rust, rails and a steam engine that's already been in a film: this yard is a gift for your camera roll. Locomotive 301 starred in Out of Africa, so give it your best close-up.
card.stand_here: Start at the phone icon on the map, right at the centre of the museum site, then wander around the open-air yard. Face the rows of locomotives and look for locomotive 301 with the rail yard behind it.
card.zoom: Use zoom 1x for most shots of the locomotives. Switch to 0.5x when you want a whole engine in the frame, and try 2x to 5x to pick out details from a distance.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, tap the locomotive, then drag the slider to make the picture a little darker so the sky and the rusty colours stay rich.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is much kinder to the engines than harsh midday sun. If you also want the jacaranda road outside, September and October are when the trees bloom.
card.selfie_here: Head to the outdoor yard and stand next to the big Garratt steam engines, which one guide calls the most impressive outdoors. Use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the engine over your shoulder. Carriage 12, the inspection coach linked to the Tsavo man-eaters, also makes a fun backdrop, so try the doorway.
card.rules_and_safety: You need an entry ticket for the museum site. Personal phone photos are generally allowed, but check the official site before you go. The yard is outdoors, so bring a hat or sunblock.
card.challenge: Find the rustiest, most colourful bit of metal in the yard and make it look like a poster.
card.good_to_know: The museum sits right beside Nairobi railway station and is run by Kenya Railways. It opened in 1971 and keeps exhibits from the old East African Railways, including early diesel locomotives and passenger coaches. A small working miniature railway was added in 2011.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Start at the phone icon on the map, right at the centre of the museum site, then wander around the open-air yard. Face the rows of locomotives and look for locomotive 301 with the rail yard behind it.

selfie_spots.detail: in the outdoor yard, standing next to the large articulated Garratt steam engines
selfie_spots.why: One guide calls the Garratts the most impressive outdoor engines, and another says there are photo ops alongside the steam engines.

selfie_research.notes: The sources describe good photo areas (the outdoor locomotive yard and the old carriages) but none names a spot where a selfie would have the museum itself behind the visitor, so the selfie spots are the best available matches and should be checked on the ground. No page names a fixed spot for a passer-by to photograph the visitor with the whole museum, so ask_someone_spot is null. The only photo rules found concern fees, not selfie sticks or tripods: one page gives a Ksh 1,000 one-person photoshoot charge and a Ksh 10,000 group charge on top of entry fees, and another says these are in-practice fees rather than official ones. The museum is on Station Road, next to Nairobi Railway Station. The jacaranda-lined boulevard leading to the museum is praised for photos, but no page names its exact location, so I left it out.

card.hook: Step up to the eastern gate on Moi Avenue and the city noise seems to drop a notch. Mature trees arch overhead and paved paths pull your eye straight into the green.
card.stand_here: Stand on Moi Avenue at the eastern entrance of Jeevanjee Gardens, about 75 m north-east of the middle of the gardens. Face south-west and look in along the paths.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the gate, trees and paths look natural. Tap 0.5x if you want more walkway and leafy canopy in the shot.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the main path along one line so it leads the eye into the park, then tap the shaded path and drag it a little darker if the bright sky behind the trees looks washed out.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning or late in the afternoon, when the light is softer.
card.selfie_here: Try the statue of Alibhai Mulla Jeevanjee on the western side, near the Muindi Mbingu Street entrance. Use the front camera at 1x or 0.5x and hold it low so the statue and trees are over your shoulder. Nobody has confirmed the backdrop, and one visitor says the statue is gone, so check on arrival.
card.rules_and_safety: Works may be going on in the park, so check current conditions before you plan your visit. It's polite not to point your phone at individuals. Don't wander the park at night.
card.challenge: Get the path on a gridline, the branches across the top and the gate edges dead straight, all without a single stranger's face in the shot.
card.good_to_know: A.M. Jeevanjee, an Asian-born entrepreneur in Kenya, founded the gardens and gave them to the people of Nairobi as a resting place. It was private property and is held in trust for the public. It's described as the only park in the city owned directly by the people, which is a nice detail for your caption.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Moi Avenue at the eastern entrance of Jeevanjee Gardens, about 75 m north-east of the middle of the gardens. Face south-west and look in along the paths.

selfie_spots.detail: at the statue, which stands on the western side near the Muindi Mbingu Street entrance
selfie_spots.why: It is a named statue inside the park, but no page describes a backdrop view from this spot, so it needs checking on arrival.

selfie_spots.detail: at the pedestal close to the eastern entrance on Moi Avenue

selfie_research.notes: Weak evidence overall. No page gives a specific selfie angle or a photographer position that frames the whole garden, so both selfie spots are inferred from named features only. One Tripadvisor reviewer says the Jeevanjee statue is no longer there, which conflicts with other pages that describe it. Airial's FAQ asks about the best photo spots but its answer only mentions mature trees and the Bunge La Mwanainchi debates, with no location. No page states selfie stick, tripod or photography rules. Sources on opening hours and the address are consistent (27 Monrovia St, 5 AM to 6 PM daily), but they are not needed for the spots.
